# Array prefetch (APB)

The array access unit (AAU) runs a small program of `fapb` entries
alongside the main instruction stream. Each entry streams one array
into a region ("area") of the array prefetch buffer (APB); the loop body
then reads the elements with `movaX` operations in four dedicated
channels instead of loads. A `mova` takes no ALU channel and has a fixed
latency, whatever the memory latency. The AAU also has stores and loads
with an address register that increments itself (`staa`, `ldaa` +
`incr`).

This page is what a compiler needs to use APB correctly: the program
format, what a `mova` reads, what stops the unit, how traps interact
with it, and what it costs. Encodings of the syllables are in
[bundle.md](bundle.md) (AAS, SS `bap`/`eap`, CS0 `ldisp`); loop mode is
in [control-transfer.md](control-transfer.md).

## Model [guide, source]

1. Write the AAU registers the program uses: array descriptors `%aadN`,
   start indices `%aaindN`, increments `%aaincrN` (`aaurw`/`aaurwd`/
   `aaurwq`, channels 2 and 5).
2. `ldisp %ctpr2, label` loads the program at `label`. Only `%ctpr2`
   can hold it.
3. `bap` ("begin array prefetch") starts it. From now on the AAU fetches
   each area's elements ahead of use, independently of the main stream.
4. In the loop, `movaX` operations read elements from the areas; a `mova`
   with `am = 1` advances its area by one step after the instruction.
5. The program ends when `%ctpr2` is overwritten (lcc writes
   `disp %ctpr2, disp=0x0` after the loop) or at the next call or return.

`eap` ("end array prefetch") pauses the program: a `bap` after it
resumes where it stopped [hw].

## The program [source: gas; hw]

An APB instruction is 16 bytes with no header: a left half (APS0 +
APLS0) and a right half (APS1 + APLS1), 8 bytes each. In assembly one
`{ }` group holds up to two `fapb` entries: the one written with `ct=`
is the left half, the one with `dpl=` the right half. gas fills an
absent half with zeros. The program follows the function's code (lcc
places it after the loop's prologue, jumped over, after `.align 8`).

```
	.align	8
.Lprog:
	{
	  fapb	ct=0, dcd=0, fmt=4, mrng=16, d=4, incr=1, ind=0, asz=3, abs=0, disp=0
	  fapb	dpl=0, dcd=0, fmt=4, mrng=16, d=3, incr=1, ind=0, asz=4, abs=0, disp=0
	}
	{
	  fapb	ct=1, dcd=0, fmt=4, mrng=16, d=2, incr=1, ind=0, asz=4, abs=16, disp=0
	}
```

APS fields (APLS is the 32-bit `disp`):

| Bits | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 31 | `ct` (left) / `dpl` (right) | `ct = 1`: last instruction of the program; it must be set in the last instruction's left half. `dpl = 1`: the right half's other fields are ignored and its area streams the same array as the left half's, with a position of its own (channels 2 and 3 read element 0, then 1, as channels 0 and 1 do) [hw]; lcc always writes 0 |
| 30 | `si` | Secondary index, v1 only; gas rejects it on v2+ |
| 28–29 | `dcd` | "Data cache disabled" (kernel `aau_context.h`; the guide's "cd", flag disabling the cache memories): 0 all caches; 1 reserved; 2 DCACHE2 off; 3 DCACHE2 and ECACHE off [guide]. Values 1–3 return the same data as 0; a stream with 2 (4C) or 3 (both) leaves other cached data alone, where 0 evicts it (Timing) [hw]. lcc always writes 0: also under `#pragma vector nontemporal`, `-fcache-opt`, `-fcache-opt-l2` and `-floop-st-dcache-mode=nocache_wc_force`, in 1.29.16 for v3, v5, v6 and in 1.31.05 [lcc]; it bypasses caches only per access, through the MAS (timing.md, "Memory") |
| 25–27 | `fmt` | Element format: 1 byte, 2 half, 3 word, 4 double, 5 quad, 7 quad packed (both qemus accept 7 as a 16-byte format; on the 4C, the Elbrus-8C2 and the 2C3 any `mova` from an area with `fmt` 7, `movaqp` or `movad`, is SIGILL `ILL_ILLOPC` at the `mova`, while `bap` itself doesn't trap (`tools/isa-probes/tagx.c` `movaqp7`, `movad7`, `nomova7`; on the 8C2 also with `mrng` 32), so it is a format of none of them). Used to scale the increment and to check alignment |
| 20–24 | `mrng` | Bytes a `mova` may read per step, from 1 to 31; 0 means 32. On v3 at most 24 + *g*, where *g* is the largest of 1, 2, 4 and 8 that divides both the area's start (base + `%aaind` + `disp`) and its step in bytes; above that every `mova` from the area is diagnostic ("Diagnostic results") [hw: 4C]. The 8C2 and the 2C3 take any `mrng` [hw] |
| 15–19 | `d` | Descriptor `%aadN` (0–31) |
| 12–14 | `incr` | Increment register `%aaincrN` (0–7); `%aaincr0` is always 1 |
| 8–11 | `ind` | Start-index register `%aaindN` (0–15); `%aaind0` is always 0 |
| 5–7 | `asz` | Area size: 64 × 2^asz bytes; gas accepts 0–5 |
| 0–4 | `abs` | Area base in the buffer, in 64-byte units; must be a multiple of the area size (gas checks) |

Instruction *i*'s left half describes **area *i*** and its right half
**area 32 + *i***, so a program has at most 32 instructions [source:
kernel `traps.c`, qemu]. The unit for `asz` and `abs` is the guide's;
no other source gives one, and lcc's programs fill each half with
exactly 32 units (`asz` 3 + 3 + 4 above = 8 + 8 + 16).

## Registers [source; lcc]

| Register | Count | Width | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `%aadN` | 32 | 128 | Array descriptor: base address in bits 0–47 of the low half (plus tag, rw bits); size in the high half up to v6 |
| `%aaindN` | 16 | 32 (v3, v4), 64 (v5+) | Start index in bytes; `%aaind0` = 0. Checked (`ind64`: base = array − 2³², index 2³²): the 8C2 reads the array, the 4C uses the low 32 bits and gets diagnostic values [hw] |
| `%aaincrN` | 8 | 32, sign-extended (v3, v4), 64 (v5+) | Step in elements; `%aaincr0` = 1. Checked (`incr64`: bytes, increment 2³² + 1): the 8C2 reads from `a + 2³² + 1`, the 4C from `a + 1` [hw] |
| `%aastiN` | 16 | as `%aaind` | Index for `staa` and `ldaa` |
| `%aaldiN`, `%aaldaN`, `%aaldv`, `%aaldm`, `%aafstr`, `%aasr` | | | Current positions and state; the kernel saves them on traps. `%aasr` has `stb` (bit 5), `iab` (bit 6) and the unit's state `lds` (bits 7–9: 0 none, 1 ready, 3 active, 5 stopped) [source: kernel `aau_regs_types.h:31-43`] |
| `%aabfN` | 16 | | Write-only; "value for modification of AAU load flags" (binutils). `aaurw,2 v, %aabfN` sets `%aasr.iab` to bit 1 of N and `%aasr.stb` to bit 0 of N; v and bits 2–3 of N don't matter, a write in channel 5 changes nothing, and `%aaldv`/`%aaldm` are untouched [hw: `isaleft.c` `bf*_sg`, the `aasr` the kernel saved in `uc_extra` at a later SIGSEGV; 4C, 8C2, 2C3]. The kernel saves and restores `%aad`, `%aaind` and `%aaincr` at a trap only while `iab` is set, and `%aasti` only while `stb` is [source: kernel `ttable.c:616-618`, `ttable-inline.h:600-605`, `aau_regs_access.h:593-603`, `:644-649`]. So a write to one with bit 1 of N clear (0, 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12, 13) **stops the program at the next trap**: the running program goes on, but after any later trap or interrupt every `mova` gives a diagnostic value, in both halves; the others (2, 3, 6, 7, …) leave `iab` set and change nothing visible. Writing a `%aad`, `%aaind` or `%aaincr` sets `iab` and writing a `%aasti` sets `stb` (with no program too); `bap`, `eap` and `ldisp` set neither (`bf0_aad_sg`, `bf0_aasti_sg`, `bf0_bap_sg`, `aa_*_sg`) |

`aaurwd` to a `%aad` sets the base and the rw bits and clears the high
half (qemu). User code can execute `aaurrd` on the 4C, but every
register read that way returned 0 [hw]; `aaurrq` of a `%aad` does read
the descriptor back: after `aaurwq` of (0x0123456789abcdef, 0x10) its
low half is `0x1800456789abcdef`, the base's 48 bits with bits 59–60
set (semantics.md, "Memory, tag and descriptor operations"; 4C and
8C2). The positions the unit keeps (`%aaldi`, ...) can't be read
directly; a signal handler finds what the kernel saved at the trap in
`uc_extra` (`aasr`, `aaldv`, `aaldm`, `aaldi[]`, `aalda[]`, `aafstr`;
`isaleft.c` prints them).

How lcc sets them up:

| | v3, v4 | v5, v6 |
|---|---|---|
| Array address | in the descriptor: `aaurwq %rN, %aadK` with the base in `%rN` and 0 in `%rN+1` | in a start index: `aaurwd %rN, %aaindK` (64-bit); the descriptor gets base 0 (`aaurw`) |
| Step | `aaurw n, %aaincr1` (elements) | `aaurwd n, %aaincr1` |

## What a mova reads [hw]

```
movaX,CH area=A, ind=I, am=M, be=B, %dst      CH = 0..3
```

Channels 0 and 1 read areas 0–31 (left halves), channels 2 and 3 areas
32–63 (right halves): `area` names the instruction, the channel picks
the half. The area's first element is at

```
start = AAD[d].base + AAIND[ind] + (unsigned 32-bit) disp
```

and each step adds `size(fmt) × AAINCR[incr]` bytes. A `mova` reads
`size(X)` bytes at `current + I`.

- **`disp` is zero-extended**: with base `lo + 64` and `disp=-64` (gas
  encodes `0xffffffc0`) the first `mova` reads `lo + 2³²`, not `lo`, on
  the 4C, 8C2 and 2C3 alike. Put a negative offset into the base or
  `%aaind`, and `disp` at 0 or above (lcc always writes `disp=0`).
- **Negative increments** (backward areas) work, but **on v3 an area may
  not go below its base**: with the base at the first element read
  (the highest) and `%aaincr1` = −1, the 4C's `movad`s give a diagnostic
  value (SIGILL at the first use), whether the increment was written
  with `aaurw` or `aaurwd`; with the base at the lowest element and the
  start in `disp` (56 for 8 doublewords; lcc's v3 code puts the base
  below the stream and its start in `%aaind`) it reads all 8 right. The
  8C2 and the 2C3 read both arrangements right (`aaurwd` of −1). Whether
  a 32-bit `aaurw` of a negative increment is sign-extended on v5+ was
  not tried on purpose: if not, the area would step 2³² elements, 32 GiB
  for doublewords (the warning below). So on v5+ write a negative
  increment with `aaurwd`, as lcc does (`pocchk2.c` `apb_*`; the
  proof-of-concept back end's I41).

| Behaviour | Observed |
|---|---|
| `am = 1` | Advances the area by one step after the instruction; several `am = 1` movas on one area in one instruction advance it once. Without `am` the area stays put |
| `ind` | Byte offset inside the step, 0–31: `mrng = 32` with `movad` at `ind` 0, 8, 16, 24 reads four consecutive doubles. On v3 it must be a multiple of the `mova`'s size ("Diagnostic results") |
| `movab`, `movah`, `movaw` | Zero-extended |
| `be = 1` | Byte-swapped; for `movaq` the whole 16 bytes |
| `movaq,0 ind=I` | Low half from `I`, high half from `I + 8` (gas writes it as two AAS entries, `ind` I and I + 8, in channels 0 and 1); `movaq,2` likewise in channels 2 and 3 (4C, 8C2, 2C3: `tagx.c` `movaq`; with `fmt` 5 the area steps 16 bytes) |
| `movaq` / `movaqp` | `movaq` fills a register pair (`%qrN`); `movaqp` is v5+: 16 bytes into one quad register (lcc uses it on v5, v6 with `fmt = 5` and `mrng` 0, or 16 where one `movaqp` reads each element). gas accepts `movaqp` for every `-mcpu` (v2–v7), but on v3 (the 4C) it does not trap: from an `fmt` 5 or 4 area it writes **a diagnostic value** (`eaed0f70eaed0f70`, tag 1 in both halves) into the low 64-bit register, and a plain use of it is SIGILL `ILL_ILLOPN` (`tagx.c` `movaqp`, `movaqp4`, `movaqp_use`). v3 code must not use it |

### Diagnostic results [hw]

While the program runs, a `mova` never traps (for one that runs after
the program stopped, see the next section). When it cannot deliver data
it writes a diagnostic value (tag 1 in both halves, bits
`eaed0f70eaed0f70`), which then behaves like any other diagnostic
operand. Cases seen:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| `ind + size > mrng` | diagnostic |
| v3: `mrng` > 24 + *g*, where *g* is the largest of 1, 2, 4 and 8 dividing both the area's start (base + `%aaind` + `disp`) and its step in bytes | **every** `mova` from the area is diagnostic, `ind` 0 included. An area stepping one element from an aligned start takes `mrng` ≤ 25 for bytes, 26 for halves, 28 for words and 32 for doublewords: 24 + the element size is always safe, since v3 already needs the start aligned to the element. A byte area stepping 8, 24 or 40 bytes from a doubleword boundary takes 32, stepping 2 bytes 26, stepping 4 or 12 bytes 28. A start 1, 2 or 4 bytes past a doubleword, set through the base, `%aaind` or `disp`, allows 25, 26 or 28. Backward areas (steps −1, −2, −8 bytes) behave as forward ones. The 8C2 and the 2C3 give data in all of these (`tools/isa-probes/pocchk3.c` `m_*`: 321 areas, each read by eight wide instructions of two movas, at `ind` 0 and at `ind` = `mrng` − size; the rule predicts every one on the 4C; the proof-of-concept back end's I48) |
| v3: a `mova` at an `ind` that is not a multiple of its own size (`movah` at `ind` 1, `movaw` at 2, `movad` at 4, in areas of their own format) | diagnostic. The 8C2 and the 2C3 return the bytes there (`m_*`, the reads at `ind` = `mrng` − size). Narrow movas at offsets aligned to their own size inside a wider element work (`movab` at 3, `movah` at 6, `movaw` at 4 in a doubleword area: `apb.c` `narrow`) |
| `mova` wider than `fmt` (`movad` on `fmt = 3`) | diagnostic (v3, v5, whatever `mrng`; v6 reads data whenever `ind` + size ≤ `mrng`, "v6") |
| Base not aligned to `fmt` (v3, and v4 by lcc's changelog) | diagnostic. lcc's code that assumes the alignment (`-faligned`, `__builtin_assume_aligned`) dies with SIGILL `ILL_ILLOPN` at the first non-speculative use of what it read (a dot product of doubles 1 or 4 bytes off: the copy of the sum into the result register), where the same v3 code runs right on the 8C2 and the 2C3 [hw: `tools/isa-probes/pocchk6.c` `align`, lcc 1.29.16 and 1.31.05]. lcc proves the alignment, versions long loops (1.31) or needs `-faligned` ("How lcc uses APB") [lcc]; v5 allows unaligned 2, 4, 8 bytes and v6 16 bytes [guide, lcc-doc] (the 8C2 reads `movaqp` from an `fmt` 5 area right at any offset 0–15: "128-bit movas (v5+)", Speed). Whatever `UPSR.ac` says: with it set, misaligned areas give the same and never trap ([x86-support.md](x86-support.md); `isaleft.c` `ac_*`) |
| Two areas whose `abs`/`asz` overlap | diagnostic |
| Element in an unmapped page | diagnostic; no signal. The prefetch running past the end of an array into an unmapped page is harmless (lcc's loops over arrays that end at a `PROT_NONE` page are correct) |

The kernel handles an AAU page fault speculatively: it maps the page if
it can and otherwise marks the access invalid, without a signal
[source: kernel `do_aau_fault`, `mm/fault.c`].

## Stores into a prefetched array [hw]

The buffer is **not kept coherent with stores**. A `mova` returns what
memory held when the unit fetched the element, and a later store to it,
ordinary (`std`) or AAU (`staad`), doesn't change what the `mova` reads
(`st_*` cases: the element is overwritten after the first `mova` of a
stream, then read a few movas later):

| Element overwritten (read by `mova` number) | 4C | Elbrus-8C2 |
|---|---|---|
| 0, right after `bap` and its 21-cycle wait | old value | old value |
| 1, 2 (also after a further 64 cycles) | old value | old value |
| 7 | old value | **new value** |
| 40 (step 5 doubles, read by the 9th `mova`) | new value | new value |

Which stores a `mova` sees depends on how far the prefetch has run, so a
compiler must treat it as unpredictable: **use APB for an array only if
nothing writes, during the loop, an element of it that a later `mova`
reads**, or, on v3–v5 only, with 1 ≤ `%lsr.ldovl` ≤ the store's
distance d in iterations (the iterations from the store to the `mova`
that reads its element; `ldovl` < d when the store is in the
iteration's `alc` instruction; measured on the 4C and 8C2 for `ldovl`
1–8). Stores to elements already read are harmless. lcc
[lcc, `-O3 -faligned`] uses APB for `a[i] = a[i] * 2` and for `a[i] =
b[i] * 2` with `restrict`; without `restrict` it versions the loop on a
run-time comparison of the pointers (`a ≤ b` among others) before the
APB version; it never uses APB for `a[i + 2] = a[i] * 2`. From a
distance of 5 elements on it does, on v5 and v6 [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3`],
with a small `ldovl`, and its v6 loops computed right although the 2C3
follows no `ldovl` rule ([loops.md](loops.md), "Stores into a streamed
array"). A small `ldovl` costs much of APB's speed in fast loops (on
the 8C2 a 2-cycle loop runs 7.4× slower at `ldovl` 1). Both qemus read
memory when the `mova` executes, so they return the stored value.

## Starting, pausing and stopping [hw]

| Between movas of one stream | Next `mova` |
|---|---|
| `call` (to a function that just returns) | **SIGILL** |
| `disp %ctpr2, ...` (any write to `%ctpr2`) | **SIGILL** |
| `eap` | **SIGILL** |
| `eap` ... `bap` | continues where it stopped |
| `disp %ctpr1, ...` | continues |
| `aaurw 0, %aabf0` | continues, until the next trap; after it, diagnostic (it clears `%aasr.iab`, Registers above) |
| a page fault or a signal handler | continues, but see "Traps" below |

A call or return resets the AAU [source: qemu `translate-ct.c`; kernel
comments in `ttable.c`], so APB can be used only in loops without calls
[guide 6.6], and a `mova` after a call (even in a later, separate loop)
must follow its own `ldisp` and `bap`. System calls also reset it (they
are reached through calls anyway). The kernel itself is built with
lcc's `-fno-loop-apb` and keeps `%ctpr2` free in trap code
([kernel-build.md](../abi/kernel-build.md), "Array prefetch, `%ctpr2`,
DAM").

After the loop lcc writes `{ disp %ctpr2, disp=0x0; aaurw,2 0, %aabf0 }`
and never uses `eap`. The `%aabf0` write clears `%aasr.iab` and
`%aasr.stb` (Registers, above), the flags that make the kernel save and
restore the AAU registers at a trap, so later traps skip that work
(inferred). Any value, written to `%aabf0` (or 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12, 13),
leaves the running stream alone, but after the next trap the unit
doesn't resume and every `mova` is diagnostic, in both halves of the
buffer (`aabf*_pf_*`, `aabfr*`, `aabf_signal`, with a page fault or a
signal handler between movas). Written before `bap`, after the register
writes, it changes nothing visible until a trap, and then kills the
stream the same way (`isaleft.c` `bf_pre_sg`); the next loop's `%aad`,
`%aaind` or `%aaincr` writes set `iab` again. A compiler should end
every APB loop as lcc does, after the loop's last `mova` and AAU store:
written earlier, a trap loses the descriptors, and a cleared `stb`
would lose live `%aasti` indices in the same way (inferred from the
kernel source).

## Traps, signals and the loop counter [hw, source]

The kernel stops the AAU on every trap and interrupt, saves its state
and restarts it on return [source: kernel `ttable.c`]. On return it does
not restore each area's position: it **recomputes** it as

```
start + step × iterations,  iterations = %ilcr.lcnt − %lsr.lcnt
                            (+ the epilogue iterations done, when lcnt
                               has reached 0 and ldmc is set)
```

(`kernel/cpu/iset_v3.c:194-196`; v6 saves the positions instead, and
on the 2C3 a trap between movas outside a loop leaves them in place:
"v6", below). So the number of `am` advances of every area must equal
the number of loop-mode iterations done, **at every instruction where
an interrupt can arrive**.
Interrupts arrive at any instruction (timer, other CPUs), so this is a
correctness rule, not a corner case. `apb-loop.c` shows it on the 4C:

| Loop (sum of 1M elements, 200 runs) | Result |
|---|---|
| `loop_mode` loop counted by `%lsr`, one `am = 1` per area per iteration, `%lsr` written before `bap` | correct in every run, also with a SIGALRM every 100 µs (about 21,000 signals) |
| Ordinary branch loop with the same movas | wrong in every run, even without extra signals |
| `loop_mode` loop, but `%lsr` written after `bap` and a page fault between them, after a 777-iteration loop | the stream is shifted by exactly 777 elements; correct without the fault |

lcc's loops (`apb-lcc.c`: one array, two arrays with a stride and an
offset, a dot product) gave 0 wrong results in 900 with about 34,000
signals, and with three processes sharing one CPU.

Epilogue iterations count too: with `ldmc` = 1 the movas keep going in
them ([loops.md](loops.md)), and a loop of `lcnt` 8 + `ecnt` 31 that
sums its 39 elements through one area (`loopF`) gave the right sum in
all of a million runs with a SIGALRM every 100 µs (about 4,900 signals
on the 4C, 2,100 on the 8C2), so the kernel's recomputation also covers
interrupts in the epilogue. With `ldmc` = 0 the movas stop and the sum
counts the eighth element 32 times, as expected.

**v6 keeps the positions** [hw: Elbrus-2C3, `apb-loop.c`]: the ordinary
branch loop is correct there in every run (0 of 200 wrong under 12,294
signals; the 8C2: 200 of 200 wrong), and the stale-counter loop with a
page fault is not shifted. So on v6 an area may advance any number of
times per iteration, in any loop (lcc 1.31's `-floop-apb-packets`,
"available from Elbrus V6"). The rules below are for v3–v5. Such a
loop must still find `%lsr` with `vlc` 0, `lcnt` above 0 or `ldmc` 1
(write it, 0 will do, before the first `mova`): on the 2C3 a `mova`
outside `loop_mode` is SIGILL while `%lsr` says an earlier counted loop
has ended ("v6", below; [hwbugs.md](hwbugs.md)).

Rules that follow (v3–v5):

- Use APB only in a loop counted by `%lsr` ([loops.md](loops.md);
  `ct %ctpr1 ? %NOT_LOOP_END`, `alc alcf=1, alct=1`), with every area
  advanced (`am = 1`) exactly once per iteration. The `loop_mode` bit
  itself is not needed: `apb-loop.c`'s `loopD`, `loopA` without it, is
  right in every run under about 20,700 signals on the 4C and 8,700 on
  the 8C2 (the PoC's pipelined kernels, which use no `loop_mode`, also
  pass).
- Write `%lsr` (which also sets `%ilcr`) before `bap`, and issue no
  `mova` outside the loop.
- In the prologue between `bap` and the loop, no area may advance.
- A `mova` in an epilogue iteration (`lcnt` 0, `ecnt` > 0) needs `ldmc`
  = 1: with `ldmc` 0 it reads nothing in a `loop_mode` instruction, and
  outside `loop_mode` it reads, but the kernel's recomputation leaves
  it out, so an interrupt there repeats an element (4–6 wrong sums in
  3,000,000 runs on the 4C and the 8C2: [loops.md](loops.md)); on the
  2C3 it is SIGILL ("v6").

## Timing [hw]

On the 4C (elbrus-v3), data in L1 or L2:

| | Cycles |
|---|---|
| `bap` → first `mova` without a stall | 22 (a `mova` issued earlier stalls in steps of 4 cycles; lcc leaves 17–24) |
| `bap` → first data from memory | about 160–250 more |
| `mova` → consumer | 5, in any channel or cluster; a consumer issued earlier stalls a fixed 4 cycles |
| `mova` issue | up to four per instruction, every cycle |

lcc's loops with and without APB (`apb-lcc.c`, ns per element at about
0.8 GHz; `-fno-loop-apb` turns APB off):

| Array | `sumd` APB | `sumd` no APB | `dot` APB | `dot` no APB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 KiB | 0.70 | 1.36 | 5.40 | 5.40 |
| 256 KiB | 0.68 | 4–18 | 5.38 | 8–23 |
| 64 MiB | 0.86 | 18.2 | 5.48 | 24.2 |

With APB the loop runs at the same speed from memory as from L1; without
it, it runs at the memory latency, since lcc's code without APB does not
prefetch. (`dot` is bound by its chain of FP additions while the data is
in L1.)


One area delivers at most **16 bytes a cycle** (4C and 8C2; lcc's
loops in timing.md, "Array prefetch"): lcc's v5 code, which reads 32
bytes an iteration from one area with two `movaqp`, runs no faster per
element than its v3 code with two `movad`.

**Area size is the prefetch depth.** `apb-stream.c` (generated by
`gen_apb_stream.py`) streams one array through one area in a
one-instruction `loop_mode` loop, one `movad` per iteration consumed six
iterations later, for every `asz` and `dcd`, in cycles per element
(best of five; memory: 4 Mi elements of a 512 MiB array, the 4C on one
NUMA node; reproducible within 1%):

| `asz` (area) | L1, 4C | L1, 8C2 | memory, 4C | memory, 8C2 | memory, a line per `mova` (step 8), 4C | the same, 8C2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (64 B) | 2.5 | 1.5 | 12.1 | 10.4 | 12.4 | 12.2 |
| 1 (128 B) | 1.25 | 1.0 | 6.2 | 5.5 | 6.4 | 5.9 |
| 2 (256 B) | 1.0 | 1.0 | 3.1 | 2.9 | 3.7 | 3.4 |
| 3 (512 B) | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.6 | 1.5 | 3.2 | 3.2 |
| 4 (1 KiB) | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.1 | 1.15 | 3.2 | 3.2 |
| 5 (2 KiB) | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.05 | 1.14 | 3.3 | 3.2 |

- From memory, each doubling of the area roughly halves the time per
  element until about 1 KiB (`asz` 4), where a stream from memory runs
  nearly as fast as from L1. A one-instruction loop needs `asz` ≥ 2
  (4C) or ≥ 1 (8C2) to run an element per cycle even from L1.
- An area fetches at most one new 64-byte line every 2 cycles from L1
  and about one every 3.2 cycles from memory (step 8), on both machines.
- `dcd` changes nothing on the 8C2. On the 4C, `dcd` 2 and 3 slow the
  line rate from memory to one every 5.5 cycles (step 8), and `dcd` 3
  also slows consecutive elements (9.4 cycles at `asz` 1–2, 6.9 at 3,
  3.05 at 4, 1.64 at 5); `dcd` 2 with consecutive elements costs
  nothing. So `dcd` 0, as lcc writes, is never faster for the stream
  itself; the other values pay off for the data around it (below).
- lcc fills each half of the buffer with 32 units (2 KiB) and gives
  arrays to the halves by turns. One array gets 2 KiB in the left half.
  Two arrays get 2 KiB each, one per half (read in channels 1 and 3).
  Three get 1 KiB + 1 KiB in one half and 2 KiB in the other, and four
  get 1 KiB each. Three areas in one half get 512 B, 512 B and 1 KiB
  (five or six arrays). PolyBench gramschmidt's loop of 18 areas gets
  128 B, 128 B and seven of 256 B in each half [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3` for
  v3.4c (`-faligned`), v5.8c2 and v6.2c3, and 1.31.05 for v3: sums over
  2–6 global arrays of `double`; gramschmidt with M = 500, N = 600].

Several arrays at once (`multi*` cases: K areas 64 MiB apart, one
`movad` from each per iteration, areas 0 and 1 in the left half, 2 and
3 in the right; cycles per iteration):

| Arrays × area | consecutive elements, memory: 4C | 8C2 | a line per element, L1: 4C, 8C2 | a line per element, memory: 4C | 8C2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 × 1 KiB | 1.10 | 1.19 | 2.0 | 3.2 | 3.2 |
| 2 × 1 KiB | 1.19 | 1.21 | 2.0 | 7.4 | 6.7 |
| 4 × 1 KiB | 1.85 | 1.75 | 2.0 | 15.1 | 14.8 |
| 2 × 512 B | 1.82 | 1.73 | 2.0 | 7.3 | 6.7 |
| 4 × 512 B | 2.39 | 2.06 | 2.0 | 14.7 | 13.6 |

The 2-cycle line limit from L1 is per area (four areas fetch four lines
in 2 cycles), but from memory all areas share one rate of about a line
every 3.2–3.75 cycles: about 14 GB/s on the 4C (0.8 GHz, two of three
memory channels populated) and 27 GB/s on the 8C2, for one core. Larger
areas still help when several streams compete (4 × 1 KiB against
4 × 512 B).

**Which half an area is in** (`tools/isa-probes/pocchk3.c` `col`,
cases from `gen_pocchk3.py`; the proof-of-concept back end's I47). The
probe is a one-instruction `loop_mode` loop that reads one or two
arrays of `long`, one `movad` from each per iteration, through areas of
512 B, 1 KiB or 2 KiB. LL puts both areas in the left half, LR one in
each half. "Columns" means all 600 columns of R × 600 matrices, 4,800
bytes a step. Each cell gives one area / LL / LR, in cycles per
iteration (columns: best of three passes, the same for every area size
within 5%, so one figure each; consecutive elements: best of five; the
4C on one NUMA node):

| Loop | Pages | 4C | 8C2 | 2C3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Columns, R = 500 | 4 KiB | 2.3 / 26.8 / 19.1 | 2.0 / 29.1 / 21.4 | 1.7–1.8 / 65–68 / 51.4 |
| Columns, R = 4,000 | 4 KiB | 17.5 / 35.6 / 32.4 | 19.7 / 46.6 / 39.5 | 47.1 / 95.0 / 86.9 |
| Columns, R = 500 | 2 MiB | 2.3 / 2.7 / 2.7 | 2.0 / 2.3 / 2.3 | 1.3 / 2.8 / 2.0 |
| Columns, R = 4,000 | 2 MiB | 2.5 / 2.9 / 2.9 | 2.1 / 2.8 / 2.8 | 1.5 / 2.8 / 1.9 |
| Consecutive elements from memory, 1 KiB areas | 4 KiB | 1.17 / 1.26 / 1.24 | 1.21 / 1.28 / 1.27 | 1.13 / 1.21 / 1.21 |
| The same, 2 KiB areas | 4 KiB | 1.05 / — / 1.10 | 1.21 / — / 1.27 | 1.13 / — / 1.22 |

- With 4 KiB pages the column walks are bound by DTLB misses
  (`apbleft.c` `col`: a table walk an element, below): 2 MiB pages make
  them 7–46 times faster. The exception is one array of 500 rows
  (2.3 MiB, 586 pages, few enough for the DTLB: below), which the 4C
  and the 8C2 walk as fast either way and the 2C3 1.4 times slower.
- With 4 KiB pages, two areas in one half run 9–40% slower than one in
  each half, on all three machines, **at any area size**. Areas of
  512 B, 1 KiB and 2 KiB give the same times within 5%, so a deeper
  prefetch doesn't hide the misses. Each half takes its areas' DTLB
  misses one at a time (below).
- With 2 MiB pages the half doesn't matter on the 4C and the 8C2. On
  the 2C3 one area in each half stays faster (1.9–2.0 against 2.8
  cycles), presumably v6's line rate per half ("v6", below).
- Consecutive elements from memory don't depend on the half. They
  depend on the area size, and only on the 4C, where 2 KiB areas are
  5–13% faster than 1 KiB ones (as the single-area table above shows).

**Why** [hw: `tools/isa-probes/apbleft.c` `col`, cases from
`gen_apbleft.py`: the same loops with 1 KiB areas, the core's monitors
counted in-process (monitors.md); per iteration, 4 KiB pages, R = 4,000
unless marked; two runs a machine, within 2%]:

| | 4C | 8C2 | 2C3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| table walks an element (`DTLB_TLU_QUERY`) | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| cycles the walker is busy a walk (`TLU_BUSY`) | 11.1 | 14.0 | 40.1 |
| one area: cycles | 17.3 | 20.1 | 47.3 |
| LR: cycles / walker busy | 32.6 / 23.4 | 39.9 / 30.8 | 88.0 / 81.6 |
| LL: cycles / walker busy | 35.8 / 23.3 | 47.0 / 30.9 | 95.8 / 81.6 |
| both areas on one page every step (b is a's next column): LR / LL | 17.4 / 20.4 | 20.3 / 23.2 | 47.6 / 48.6 |
| a column walk and a consecutive stream: one half / both halves | 18.0 / 17.4 | 21.0 / 20.3 | 46.0 / 47.5 |
| R = 500: table walks an iteration, one area / LL / LR | 0.01 / 1.57 / 1.19 | 0.01 / 1.57 / 1.19 | 0.01 / 1.54 / 1.18 |

- The DTLB has 256 lines of 4 entries (the kernel's "sets"), the fourth
  kept for large pages [source: kernel
  `arch/e2k/include/asm/tlb_regs_types.h:45-50`], so 768 entries hold
  4 KiB pages. One area walking a 500-row matrix (586 pages) makes
  almost no table walks; two such matrices (1,172 pages) make 0.6–0.8 an
  element, and at R = 4,000 (4,688 pages a matrix) every element is a
  table walk. With 2 MiB pages there are none (`DTLB_TLU_QUERY` 0).
- Two areas keep the walker busy twice as long as one, whichever half
  they are in. The walks don't overlap (inferred: LR takes longer than
  its two walks end to end, where overlapping walks would let it run
  near one area's time).
- One half takes its areas' misses in turn, so LL costs about twice one
  area (4C 35.8 against 2 × 17.3). LR costs the walker's time plus about
  9 cycles (2C3 6), where one area costs its walk plus 6 (2C3 7): the
  halves overlap the rest.
- When both areas need the same page every step, one walk serves both
  (`DTLB_TLU_QUERY` 1.0 an iteration) and LR runs as fast as one area.
  In LL the second area's lookup comes after the walk and hits the DTLB
  (`DTLB_HIT` 2.0 against 1.0 an iteration on the 4C and 8C2), yet costs
  3 more cycles (2C3 1).
- A consecutive stream, which never misses, slows a walking area in its
  own half by about 4% and in the other half by about 1% on the 4C and
  8C2, and not at all on the 2C3.
- At R = 500, where the DTLB holds part of the two matrices, LL also
  makes a third more table walks than LR, on all three machines, which
  adds to its cost. Why the order of the lookups changes what the DTLB
  keeps is not known.
- Every lost cycle is a 4-cycle E2 stall step (`BUB_E2`), all of them
  counted as `STALL_AAU` ("decode blocked by the AAU" in the kernel's
  Events.json).
- On the 2C3, `DTLB_HIT` stays about 0 for walking areas, where the 4C
  and 8C2 count one hit an element.

So spread a few areas over both halves, as lcc does. It costs nothing,
lets each area be 2 KiB, and avoids the slowdown of two column walks in
one half.

**Several cores** (`apb-stream one CASE T`: copies pinned to cores,
starting together, the timed loop only, mean of 40 runs from memory; a
line per element, cycles per line per core):

| Cores | 8C2 | 8C2 total | 4C, one node | 4C total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3.2 | 30 GB/s | 3.4 | 15 GB/s |
| 2 | 3.9 | 49 GB/s | 6.1 | 17 GB/s |
| 4 | 6.3 | 61 GB/s | 12.2 | 17 GB/s |
| 8 | 13.7 | 56 GB/s | | |

Consecutive elements reach the same totals (8 cores of the 8C2: 1.73
cycles per element each, 55 GB/s; 4 cores of a 4C node: 1.74, 15 GB/s).
One 4C core nearly saturates its node's memory (two DDR3 channels
populated); the 8C2 (four DDR4 channels) needs about four cores.

**`dcd` and other cached data** (`apb-stream hot CASE KB`: reread a
working set, one load a line, before and after streaming 32 MiB through
one 1 KiB area; ns per line, best of five; the 4C on one node):

| Working set | 4C `dcd` 0 | 4C `dcd` 2, 3 | 8C2 `dcd` 0 | 8C2 `dcd` 2 | 8C2 `dcd` 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 48 KiB | 8.4 → 31 | 8.4 → 10.3–10.7 | 5.2 → 117 | 5.3 → 120 | 5.3 → 6.1 |
| 256 KiB | 18.8 → 121 | 18.8 → 18.8 | 12.3 → 108 | 11.9 → 113 | 9.7 → 16.4 |
| 1 MiB | 18.7 → 120 | 18.7 → 19–33 | 23.5 → 104 | 23.5 → 116 | 23.9 → 24.1 |
| 4 MiB | memory both ways | memory both ways | 24.2 → 105 | 24.0 → 109 | 24.0 → 24.0 |

A stream with `dcd` 0 evicts everything, on the 8C2 also a working set
in L3. `dcd` 2 keeps it on the 4C and does nothing on the 8C2; `dcd` 3
keeps L1, L2 and L3 on the 8C2. Combined with the speeds above: for a
large array read once, `dcd` 2 on the 4C (consecutive elements: no
cost) and `dcd` 3 on the 8C2 (no cost at all) protect the rest of the
cache; lcc never does this. Data read with them is not cached for a
later loop either.

**Plain loads beside an area** (`pocchk3.c` `bk`; the proof-of-concept
back end's I49). The probe is a one-instruction `loop_mode` loop at
II 4 summing `a[i] × b[…]` with `fmuld` and `faddd`. Each array is read
through an area (A) or by an `ldd` into the rotating registers 12
iterations (48 cycles) before its use (P), and b runs backward
(`b[n − 1 − i]`) unless marked forward. Arrays are 8 KiB (L1), 160 KiB
(L2) or fresh stretches of 32 MiB (memory). Cycles per iteration (L2:
best of five warm runs; memory: best of three stretches), the range
covering 4 KiB and 2 MiB pages; every sum checked:

| a, b | 4C L2 | 4C memory | 8C2 L2 | 8C2 memory | 2C3 L2 | 2C3 memory |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P, P | 4.00 | 7.8–7.9 | 4.00 | 14.8–14.9 | 4.00 | 15.7–16.0 |
| P, P forward | 4.00 | 6.9–7.0 | 4.00 | 12.6–12.8 | 4.00 | 12.5–12.8 |
| —, P (b alone) | 4.00 | 6.7 | 4.00 | 11.1–11.6 | 4.00 | 11.8–12.0 |
| A, P | **5.25** | 7.2–7.3 | 4.00–4.19 | 11.4 | 4.50 | 12.9–13.0 |
| A, P forward | **5.25** | 7.5–7.6 | 4.00–4.16 | 11.6–12.1 | 5.25 | 12.0–12.1 |
| P, A | **5.25** | 7.5 | 4.00–4.13 | 11.5–11.6 | 5.25 | 12.9–13.0 |
| A, `ldd` of one address (an L1 hit) | 4.00 | 4.05 | 4.00 | 4.02 | 4.00 | 4.02 |
| A, A (b's base at its lowest element, the start in `%aaind`, increment −1) | 4.00 | 4.05 | 4.00 | 4.02 | 4.00 | 4.02 |
| P, P, 24 iterations (96 cycles) ahead | 4.00 | 5.8–5.9 | 4.00 | 10.8–11.3 | 4.00 | 12.2–12.5 |
| A, P, 24 ahead | **5.25** | 6.4–6.5 | 4.00–4.17 | 10.3–10.4 | 4.50 | 11.7–12.1 |

- From L1 every variant runs at II 4 (4.01).
- On the 4C, an area streaming beside plain loads that miss L1 costs
  those loads 1.25 cycles an iteration in L2 (10 for each 64 bytes of
  the plain stream: the monitors below). This holds whichever way
  either stream runs, for a 512 B or a 2 KiB area, and with the load in
  ALC2, 3 or 5.
  Plain loads that hit L1 pay nothing. From memory such a loop runs no
  faster than its plain stream alone (A, P 7.2–7.3 against 6.7), and
  with the plain loads 24 iterations ahead it is still 10% slower than
  two plain streams (6.4–6.5 against 5.8–5.9). The 2C3 pays 0.5–1.25
  cycles an iteration in L2, the 8C2 at most 0.2 (nothing with 2 MiB
  pages).
- With every stream in an area, the backward one included, the loop
  keeps II 4 from L1, L2 and memory on all three machines. From memory
  that is 1.4–4 times faster than any variant with a plain stream.

**What the monitors show** [hw: `tools/isa-probes/apbleft.c` `bk`, cases
from `gen_apbleft.py`: these loops and variants, counted in-process;
2 MiB pages; cycles an iteration / `STALL_AAU` stall steps an iteration;
arrays in L2 unless marked; two runs a machine]:

| a, b | 4C | 8C2 | 2C3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| —, P (b alone) | 4.00 / 0 | 4.00 / 0 | 4.00 / 0 |
| A, P | 5.25 / 0.31 | 4.00 / 0.04 | 4.50 / 0.125 |
| A, P forward | 5.25 / 0.31 | 4.00 / 0.04 | 5.25 / 0.31 |
| an area of step 0 (every `mova` reads a[0]), P | 5.24 / 0.31 | 4.00 / 0.02 | 4.50 / 0.125 |
| an area the loop never reads (the program runs, no `mova`), P | 4.00 / 0 | 4.00 / 0 | 4.00 / 0 |
| A from memory, P | 5.24 / 0.32 | 4.02 / 0.05 | 4.48 / 0.13 |
| A, P with `mas=0x20` (no L1 fill: timing.md, "Memory") | 4.79 / 0.21 | 4.00 / 0.04 | 4.79 / 0.21 |
| A, a backward stream of `ldaad` | 5.00 / 0.25 | 4.00 / 0.04–0.06 | 5.00 / 0.25 |
| —, the `ldaad` stream; A, an `ldd` that hits L1 | 4.00 / 0 | 4.00 / 0 | 4.00 / 0 |
| A with `dcd` 2 or 3, or `asz` 0 | 5.25 / 0.31 | 4.00 / ≤ 0.05 | 4.50 / 0.125 |
| both from memory (n = 4 Mi): —, P / A, P / an area of step 0, P | 6.69 / 7.32 / 7.27 | 11.0 / 11.5 / 11.0 | 12.0 / 13.1–13.3 / 12.1 |

- Every lost cycle is a 4-cycle E2 stall step (`BUB_E2`) that the core
  counts as `STALL_AAU` (0x113, "decode blocked by the AAU" in the
  kernel's Events.json); in L2 none is a wait for load data
  (`BUB_E2_MEM` 0).
- It takes an area that is fetching and loads that go to L2. Plain
  loads that miss L1, loads with `mas=0x20` and AAU loads all suffer it;
  loads that hit L1 don't. An area the loop never reads fills once and
  stops fetching (`DTLB_AAU_QUERY` 0, against 0.25 an iteration for a
  streaming area), and costs nothing.
- What the area fetches doesn't matter: an area of step 0, which
  fetches a[0] again at every step (`DTLB_AAU_QUERY` 1 an iteration),
  costs the same as one streaming from L2 or from memory, and `dcd` 2
  or 3 or a 64-byte area change nothing.
- For each 32 bytes of the plain stream the 4C loses 1.25 stall steps
  (5 cycles), 1 with AAU loads and 0.85 with `mas=0x20`; the 2C3 0.5
  steps for a backward stream and 1.25 for a forward one. Three of every
  four of the stream's 8-byte loads go to L2 (2C3 `L1_LD_MISS` 0.75 an
  iteration).
- So the area's requests and the L2-bound loads share something that
  the AAU holds (inferred; the monitors don't name it).
- From memory, on the 4C the stall takes the place of part of the
  memory wait (`STALL_AAU` 0.46 and `BUB_E2_MEM` 0.42 an iteration,
  against 0.65 of memory wait alone: 7.3 against 6.7 cycles), and an
  area of step 0 costs the same. On the 2C3 the stall stays small
  (0.09) and the extra time is longer memory waits (`BUB_E2_MEM` 2.25
  against 1.98), which an area of step 0 doesn't cause (12.1 against
  12.0): there the area's stream competes for memory (inferred).

So read all of a loop's streams through areas where possible. On v3,
when a loop must keep one stream in plain loads (alignment unknown, a
gather), areas for the other streams gain little or nothing once that
stream misses L1.

## AAU stores [lcc, source, hw]

`staa{b,h,w,d,q}` (channels 2 and 5) store to `AAD[d].base +
AASTI[ind] + literal`; an `incr,CH %aaincrN` on the next line (encoded
in the CDS AM2/AM5 bit) adds `AAINCR[N] × size` to `AASTI[ind]` after
the store. lcc uses them for stores in APB loops (`d[i] = a[i] + 1`:
`staad %b[15], %aad1[ %aasti1 ]`, `incr,5 %aaincr2`). They do not need
`bap`. On the 4C (`tools/isa-probes/loops.c`, `aastores*`): with
`aaurwd` of the base to `%aad0` and 0 to `%aasti1`, `staad,5 v, %aad0[
%aasti1 ]` with `incr,5 %aaincr0` stores consecutive doublewords, and
in a `loop_mode` instruction it obeys the loop-mode store rules like
any store, **including its `incr`**: a suppressed `staa` doesn't advance
the index, so the first iteration after the prologue stores at element 0
([loops.md](loops.md)).

Other formats on the 4C (`aastores{b,h,w,q}*`, `aastores_lit`):
`staab`, `staah` and `staaw` store the low 8, 16 and 32 bits of their
register and step 1, 2 and 4 bytes, under the same loop-mode rules (with
`pcnt` 3 and `strmd` 1, iterations 4–7 land in elements 0–3); a literal
(`%aad0[ %aasti1 + 0x8 ]`) is a byte offset added to the address (one
doubleword further), the index stepping as without it; `staaq %qrN` stores `%drN` at
the lower and `%drN+1` at the higher address and steps 16 bytes (the
area 16-byte aligned). In loop mode a `staaq` counts as two stores for
`strmd`, and splitting it raises SIGILL ([loops.md](loops.md)). With
its data ready it costs what a `staad` does; with the data written by
integer ops two cycles before, the loop took 4 more cycles per
iteration (one stall step; not analysed further) [hw].

**AAU stores need no alignment**, unlike the movas of array prefetch on
v3: `staad` from a base 1, 2 or 4 bytes off a doubleword and `staaw` 2
bytes off a word, four elements with `incr %aaincr0`, write exactly the
right bytes at the misaligned addresses and nothing else, with no signal,
on the 4C, 8C2 and 2C3 (`tools/isa-probes/pocchk2.c` `staad_mis`,
`staaw_mis`; the proof-of-concept back end's I43). So a compiler may use
AAU stores for arrays of unknown alignment on every version; only the
loads through APB need aligned elements on v3 and v4 (above). `staah` at
+1, `staaw` at +1 and `staaq` at +1, +2, +4 and +8 also write exactly
the right bytes, on all three (`tools/isa-probes/apbleft.c` `st_*`).
v5's `staaqp` doesn't: not 16-byte aligned (+1, +2, +4, +8) it is
SIGBUS (`BUS_ADRALN`) on the 8C2 and writes nothing, as `stqp` does; the
2C3 stores it at any offset. What misaligned AAU stores cost: the same
as `st*` (timing.md, "Misaligned loads and stores").

**MAS.** AAU stores take a MAS as `std` does [hw:
`tools/isa-probes/memleft.c` `values`; 4C, 8C2, 2C3]. `staad` with
0x20, 0x40 or 0x60, in ALC2 or ALC5, writes the same bytes as without
one (four elements with `incr %aaincr0`); 0x8 byte-swaps each element;
`staaw`, `staaq` and (v5+) `staaqp` take 0x60. lcc's `#pragma vector
nontemporal` loops store with `staad … mas=0x60` in a `loop_mode` loop:
on v5 and v6 their loads come through APB (`movad`), on v3 they are
ordinary `ldd,sm` and no APB program runs [lcc]. The hint works there
as on `std` (timing.md, "Cache hints in the MAS").

A warning from the 8C2: an area whose increment carried a `mova` 32 GiB
past its array (into unmapped memory) did not give a diagnostic value
as nearer unmapped addresses do; the process spun in the kernel
(nearly all system time, no page faults) until killed. The probe now
maps the page its 64-bit step reaches; don't point APB areas that far
on shared machines.

## AAU loads [hw, source, lcc]

`ldaa{b,h,w,d,q}` (and `ldaaqp`, v5+; channels 2 and 5) load from where
`staa*` would store: `AAD[d].base + AASTI[ind] + literal`. An
`incr,CH %aaincrN` beside one advances the index after the load, as
after a store: two `ldaad` with `incr,5 %aaincr0` beside the first read
consecutive doublewords. A load from a page the program may not read is
SIGSEGV (`SEGV_ACCERR`), as for `ldd`; for `ldaaq` its `si_addr` is the
address + 8 (`ldaaqp`: the address) [hw: `apbleft.c` `values`]. lcc
1.29.16 emits no AAU loads: four `-O3` loops built for v3, v5 and v6
have none (its loops read arrays through APB or ordinary loads), and
lcc-usage.yaml has no `aaurr*` (objdump's name for `ldaad`, `ldaaw` and
`ldaaq`), `ldaab`, `ldaah` or `ldaaqp` [lcc].

With a MAS [hw: `tools/isa-probes/memleft.c` `values`, cases from
`gen_memleft.py` (`ldaad` in ALC2 and ALC5, `ldaaq` and, on the 8C2 and
2C3, `ldaaqp`), and `tools/isa-probes/apbleft.c` `values`, cases from
`gen_apbleft.py` (`ldaab`, `ldaah` and `ldaaw` with each MAS, and every
width's `,sm` forms with a cache hint or `be`, each in ALC2 and ALC5);
each against a readable page, an untouched page and one the process may
not read; 4C, 8C2 and 2C3 alike except where shown]:

| MAS | `ldaa*` | `ldaa*,sm` |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ordinary load | semi-speculative: pages in an untouched page; a page it may not read gives the diagnostic value |
| 0x20, 0x40, 0x60 | ordinary load; the cache hints act as on `ldd` (timing.md, "Cache hints in the MAS") | semi-speculative, as with 0 |
| 0x8 (`be`), 0x68 | byte-swapped: each element's bytes reversed (`ldaab` unchanged); `ldaaq` and `ldaaqp` reverse all 16 bytes, so the first register of `ldaaq`'s pair gets bytes 15–8, as `movaq` with `be` | the same, semi-speculative |
| mod 2, 3 | **an ordinary load, not a DAM check**: after a lock load (`ldd,0,sm … mas=0x4`) of the same register it reads its own address and never sets `%MLOCK`, where an `ldd,5 … mas=0x3` in its place keeps the early value (`dam_aa03_*`) | mod 3 (also 0x23): fully speculative (diagnostic also for an untouched page) |
| mod 4, 7 (also 0x24, 0x27) | — | v3, v5: **`ldaab`, `ldaah`, `ldaaw`, `ldaad` and `ldaaqp` give the diagnostic value for every address**, valid pages included; `ldaaq` (a register pair, tried in ALC2): mod 4 semi-speculative, mod 7 fully speculative. v6: every width behaves as `ldaaq` |

`ldaab`, `ldaah` and `ldaaw` write the whole 64-bit register,
zero-extended (under `dbl = 0` too). The diagnostic value is a failed
load's, `4afafafa4afafafa` with tag 1 in both halves, on all three
machines (speculation.md; v6's movas give another, "v6" below).

**Misaligned AAU loads work on every version** [hw: `apbleft.c`
`mis_*`; 4C, 8C2, 2C3]. `ldaah` at +1, `ldaaw` at +1 and +2, `ldaad` at
+1, +2, +4 and +7 (the offset in the base, in `%aasti1` or in the
literal) and `ldaaq` at +1, +4 and +8 return the bytes there, plain or
`,sm`, also on the 4C, where the movas of array prefetch need aligned
elements. One that crosses into a page the process may not read is
SIGSEGV with `si_addr` the first byte of that page; its `,sm` form gives
the diagnostic value, and for `ldaaq,sm` only the register whose 8
bytes reach into that page is diagnostic, the other gets its data.
v5's `ldaaqp` is the exception: not 16-byte aligned, it is SIGBUS
(`BUS_ADRALN`, `si_addr` the instruction) on the 8C2, as `ldqp` is, and
its `,sm` form gives the diagnostic value; the 2C3 reads it at any offset (across into
a page it may not read: SIGSEGV, or wholly diagnostic with `,sm`).
Misaligned AAU accesses cost what `ld*` and `st*` do, except that an AAU
load's latency grows only when it crosses a 32-byte line (timing.md,
"Misaligned loads and stores").

In a `loop_mode` loop with the APB program running (`movad` → `staad`,
plus a sum through `ldaad`; 8 iterations, run twice), every combination
tried works: stores with 0, 0x20, 0x40 and 0x60; loads with 0, 0x2,
0x3, 0x20, 0x40 and 0x60; `,sm` loads with 0 and 3. The exception is
`ldaad,sm` with mod 4 or 7 on v3 and v5: its diagnostic value reaches
the sum, which is SIGILL `ILL_ILLOPN` (`apb_st60_ld04sm`,
`apb_st60_ld07sm`; on the 2C3 these work).

MCST's qemu does not run AAU loads: `ldaa*` are `E2K_DEF_OP_AL_UNIMPL`
(`target/e2k/operations.h.inc:1165-1169,1218`). Its MAS decoder for them
(`e2k_parse_mas_lds1` with `is_aa`, used only to step the index,
`tcg/translate-mem.c:1819-1828`) agrees with v3–v5: mod 2 and 3 are
normal; with `,sm`, mod 4 and 7 are reserved for a non-quad load in
ALC2/5 and speculative for `ldaaq` [source].

**AAU loads are slow.** Their result reaches an integer consumer 9
cycles after issue on the 4C, 11 on the 8C2 and 13 on the 2C3, each
machine's L2 hit, with MAS 0 or 0x60 and from ALC2 as from ALC5: they
pay no cluster-crossing cost. `ldd` takes 3, 3 and 5 cycles in its
cluster and 4, 4 and 5 across (`memleft.c` `timing`, `t_use_*`). These
were measured with the line in L1; a line only in L2 presumably costs
the same (inferred). A stream of AAU loads leaves no line in L1
(timing.md, "Memory"). So AAU loads are served from L2, as `ldqp` is on
v5 (inferred): use them only where a load's latency doesn't matter.

Two AAU loads in one wide instruction issue every cycle in a stream.
Two that read the same 64-byte line again in every instruction take 2
cycles, aligned or misaligned inside a 32-byte line, on all three
machines, where two aligned `ldd` take 1; two `ldaaw` 4 bytes apart
take 1 only when they straddle a 64-byte boundary [hw: `apbleft.c`
`cost`, `s_ldaad2`, `t_ldaad2`, `t_ldaaw2`, `t_ldaah2`].

## 128-bit movas (v5+) [hw: Elbrus-8C2]

`movaqp,N area=…, ind=…, am=…, be=…, %qprM` (`apb.c` built with
`-DAPB_V5`, cases `q5*`) with an area of `fmt` 5 returns 16 bytes per
element into all of `%qprM` and steps 16 bytes. A base misaligned by 8
or by 4 bytes still returns the right (unaligned) 16 bytes, as v5's
doubleword movas do with a misaligned base (the 4C gives a diagnostic
value there), and so does a base at any offset 0–15 on the 8C2 and the
2C3 ("Speed", below). `be = 1` reverses all 16 bytes (the low half of
the result is the swapped high doubleword). An area with `fmt` 7 makes
the `movaqp` (any `mova`) SIGILL `ILL_ILLOPC` on the 8C2, the 2C3 and
the 4C (the `fmt` field, above).

On v5 `movaqp` gives data only from an `fmt` 5 area with `mrng` 16 or
more (0 is 32): from `fmt` 1–4 it is diagnostic whatever `mrng`, as any
`mova` wider than its area's format is there; v6 reads it from those
too ("v6"). `mrng` 8 is diagnostic on both (`ind` + 16 > `mrng`), so a
compiler sets `mrng` ≥ `ind` + 16, as lcc's 0 and 16 do [hw: `isaleft.c`
`q_*`; 8C2, 2C3].

**Speed** [hw: `tools/isa-probes/foldp93.c`, cases from
`gen_foldp93.py`; the 8C2 and the 2C3, 2026-10-16: two runs on each
machine at offsets 0, 4 and 8, and the 0–15 run twice on the 8C2 and
once on each 2C3 core]: a misaligned base costs nothing. A
one-instruction `loop_mode` loop reads one area (`asz` 5) from a base 0
to 15 bytes off a 16-byte boundary and sums what it reads (the sums are
checked, right at every offset); cycles a step, best of five, for 512
steps from L1 and 1 Mi steps from memory:

| A step | 8C2, L1 | 8C2, memory | 2C3, L1 | 2C3, memory |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| one `movaqp`, `fmt` 5 (16 bytes) | 1.02 | 1.15–1.20 | 1.02 | 1.05 |
| two `movaqp` of one area, `ind` 0 and 16 (32 bytes; lcc's sum loops) | 2.02 | 2.29–2.41 | 1.03 | 1.42–1.43 |
| two `movad`, `fmt` 4, `ind` 0 and 8 (the same 16 bytes as halves) | 1.02 | 1.15–1.21 | 1.02 | 1.05 |
| one `movaqp` from an `fmt` 4 area (v6 only, "v6") | — | — | 1.02 | 1.05 |

Every offset gives the same figures from L1 to the hundredth; from
memory the runs differ by up to 0.12 cycle whatever the offset. So on
v5 too a stream of 16-byte elements of any alignment can be read with
one `movaqp` an element, as fast as an aligned one and as two `movad`;
only stores need 16-byte alignment on v5 (`staaqp`, "AAU stores"). The
two-`movaqp` row is the area's limit ("Timing"; "v6": 16 bytes a cycle
on v5, 32 on v6).

lcc's v5 code reads such streams so: `x[k] = x[k] − y[k] × z[k]`
through `restrict` pointers of unknown alignment is three `movaqp` from
`fmt` 5 areas (`mrng` 16) and a `qpfmul_subd` a step, the result
stored as two `staad`, its low half and, after `qpswitchd`, its high
half at + 8. With `-faligned`, and over rows of global arrays, lcc
versions the loop on the address (`cmpandedb`, bit 3) between a loop
with `staaqp` and one with `movad` and `staad` [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3`,
v5.8c2 and v6.2c3: `tools/isa-probes/foldp93_slp.c`, `pr` and `gl`].

## How lcc uses APB [lcc, guide]

- At `-O2` and above (not `-O1`), also when software pipelining is
  off (`-fswp-maxopers=0`, guide 6.3.6), for counted loops with no calls whose loads have an address linear in
  the iteration (`a[i]`, `a[k*i + c]`, `p++`, structure fields); reads
  of up to 32 bytes per array per iteration (more are split into
  several areas). Up to 32 arrays and 8 increments [guide 6.6]. lcc's v3
  code stops at 32 areas (NPB SP's xi-flux loop: 32 areas and 5 plain
  loads); its v5 and v6 code reads more arrays through one descriptor
  with the start addresses in `%aaind` (that loop: all 37 loads, 22
  descriptors and 15 `%aaind` indices) [lcc; the PoC's P57].
- On v3 and v4 it needs alignment of 2-, 4- and 8-byte elements: at
  `-O3` and `-O4` it uses APB only where it can prove it (global arrays,
  a pointer passed through `__builtin_assume_aligned`) or with
  `-faligned` or `-ffast`, which let it assume it (also per function:
  `__attribute__ ((optimize ("-faligned")))`); a loop over a plain
  pointer gets no APB (lcc 1.29.16 for v3, v3.4c, v4.1c+ and v4.8c).
  lcc 1.31 adds a run-time test, `-floop-apb-align-versioning`, on by
  default, for innermost loops "with a sufficiently large number of
  iterations", since V2–V4 can prefetch only reads whose alignment is
  proven statically or dynamically [lcc-doc: changelog 1.30]. At `-O3`
  (not `-O2`) a loop of 100,000 iterations over a pointer of unknown
  alignment tests `p & 7` (`cmpandedb`) and branches to a copy of the
  loop without APB when it isn't 0; a loop of unknown count gets no
  test, and NPB gets none (the same programs with
  `-fno-loop-apb-align-versioning`) [lcc 1.31.05 for v3 and v4.8c].
  1.30.03 also added `-faligned-apb` (assume every read of an innermost
  loop aligned, for APB only) and `#pragma apb_aligned` (the same for
  the next loop) [lcc-doc]: with either, a dot product over two
  pointers gets APB at `-O3`, the pragma also at `-O2` [lcc 1.31.05 for
  v3]. On v5 and v6 it uses APB for the same loops without any of
  these.
  Arrays of single bytes (`unsigned char a[]`, `signed char a[]`)
  never got APB in our probes, on v3, v5 or v6 [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3` for
  v3.4c, v5.8c2 and v6.2c3: sums over global byte arrays]; byte fields
  of larger records do (next item).
- On v3 it keeps to the `mrng` limit ("Diagnostic results"). A loop
  reading the first and last element of 32-byte records of bytes,
  halves or words reads each record through an area of `mrng` 32,
  because the start and the step are doubleword-aligned. For bytes 3
  and 28 of 32-byte records (a start 3 bytes off a doubleword, so at
  most 25) its loop, unrolled by two, reads two records through three
  areas of `mrng` 1, 8 and 1 (the middle one holds byte 28 of the first
  record and byte 3 of the second), where its v5 and v6 code uses an
  area of `mrng` 26 per record (`disp` 3 and 35) [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3` for
  v3.4c, v5.8c2 and v6.2c3, and 1.31.05 for v3; global arrays of
  structures].
- Backward streams (`b[n − 1 − i]`) go through areas too. On v3 the
  descriptor's base is the lowest element read, the start goes in
  `%aaind` and `%aaincr` gets −1 by `aaurw`. On v5 and v6 the
  descriptor's base is 0, the start goes in `%aaind` and the increment
  is written by `aaurwd` of −1. A forward and a backward array get one
  area per half [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3`, `s += a[i] * b[n - 1 - i]` over
  global arrays; PolyBench durbin's two loops with `-faligned` on v3,
  and as is on v5]. On v3 an array whose alignment lcc can't prove
  stays with plain loads beside the other arrays' areas in the same
  loop: for `g[i] * p[n - 1 - i]` (and `g[i] * p[i]`) with `g` global
  and `p` a pointer, `g` goes through an area and `p` is read by `ldd`
  scheduled for L1, at II 4 [lcc 1.29.16 `-O3` for v3.4c]. On the 4C
  that costs the plain loads' L2 hits 1.25 cycles an iteration ("Plain
  loads beside an area"). Without `-faligned` durbin's two loops get no
  APB on v3.
- It always writes `dcd = 0` (`-O3`, `-O4`, `-ffast`, `#pragma vector
  nontemporal`; v3, v5, v6).
- Prologue: `ldisp`, the AAU writes, `rwd %lsr`, the first iterations'
  elements loaded with ordinary `ld` into the rotating registers, then
  `bap` and a `ct %ctpr1` into the loop.
- The movas write rotating registers (`%b[]`), which the loop's
  consumers read several iterations later.
- `-fno-loop-apb` disables it; glibc's E2K string functions use
  `#pragma noprefetch` or `#pragma loop count` to stop lcc from using it
  on short loops.

### What lcc's alignment rule costs [lcc; hw: 4C]

NPB 3.0 class W, lcc 1.29.16 `-O3` unless noted: array prefetch
programs per benchmark and, on the 4C, seconds (`Time in seconds`,
three runs and two more of CG and FT, under the timing lock; every run
verified):

| Build | CG | FT | MG | LU | SP | BT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v3.4c (and generic v3) | 7 | 5 | 14 | 73 | 267 | 58 |
| v3.4c `-faligned` | 23 | 12 | 22 | 78 | 267 | 58 |
| v3.4c `-O2` | 4 | 3 | 9 | 38 | 163 | 50 |
| v5.8c2 and v6.2c3 (no alignment rule) | 22 | 13 | 22 | 78 | 266 | 58 |
| 1.31.05 v3, with or without `-fno-loop-apb-align-versioning` | 5 | 6 | 15 | 74 | 262 | 62 |
| 1.31.05 v3 `-faligned-apb` | 21 | 13 | 28 | 78 | 262 | 62 |
| 4C, v3.4c | 3.00–3.11 s | 0.92–0.94 s | 1.97–1.98 s | | | |
| 4C, v3.4c `-faligned` | 1.53–1.54 s | 0.62–0.63 s | 1.79–1.80 s | | | |

SP and BT keep their arrays global, so the rule costs them nothing.
CG's kernel `conj_grad` reads its vectors through pointer parameters and
gets no program under the rule, 12 with `-faligned`. On the 4C
`-faligned` makes CG 2.0× and FT 1.48× faster, and the gain is array
prefetch's: with `-fno-loop-apb` the plain build takes 3.04–3.13,
0.92–0.93 and 1.96 s and the `-faligned` one 3.03–3.11, 0.92–0.93 and
1.87–1.92 s (part of MG's gain is not APB's). The price of assuming is
the trap in "Diagnostic results" for data that isn't aligned.

## Generations [lcc-doc]

| ISA | Capability |
|---|---|
| v2–v4 | Only loads aligned to their size; lcc proves alignment statically or, from 1.30, versions long loops on it at run time ("How lcc uses APB") |
| v5 | Unaligned loads; 64-bit `%aaind`; loads of different sizes from one array can share one prefetch area; `movaqp` |
| v6 | Strides that are not a multiple of the load size; the head of a prefetch area can advance several times per iteration; the kernel saves `%aaldi` directly (lcc 1.31; all three checked on the 2C3: "v6", below) |

Loops on v5+ also have a 64-bit hardware loop counter (lcc 1.25), so lcc
no longer splits loops whose trip count may not fit in 32 bits.

## Hardware bug in code placement [source]

`CPU_HWBUG_CODE_PLACEMENT` (MCST bugs 146897, 140436, 77417; E2S, E8C,
E1CP, E8C2, E12C, E16C, E2C3 rev ≤ 1): jumps to the end of a 4 KiB page
"and placement of asynchronous program code" can misbehave; branch
targets and return addresses must avoid page offsets 0xdc0–0xdf8 and
0xee0–0xff8 (kernel `cpu_features.h`). MCST gas works around it by
default for v2–v6 (`ENABLE_FIX_LCC_BUG_142105`): it moves labels and
call return addresses out of those ranges and aligns code sections to
1 KiB. The rule for the APB program itself is not published. Other
errata and our own unconfirmed observations (one on APB programs on the
2C3) are in [hwbugs.md](hwbugs.md).

## Emulators

Neither qemu buffers anything: both read memory when the `mova`
executes, and neither models buffer areas, alignment on v3 or timing.
Of `apb.c`'s first 76 cases MCST's qemu matches the 4C in 63, the
community qemu in 64; all address arithmetic, `am`, `ind`, `be`, narrow movas,
the halves and the areas agree. Differences:

| Case | 4C | MCST's qemu | Community qemu |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signal handler during a `loop_mode` APB loop | correct | **wrong data**: `sigreturn` restarts every area from its start (`linux-user/e2k/signal.c`); lcc's loops in `apb-lcc.c` give 600 wrong results of 900 | correct |
| Trap between movas outside loop mode | position from the loop counters | continues | continues |
| `ind + size > mrng`, `mova` wider than `fmt` | diagnostic | diagnostic (other bits) | data; SIGILL |
| `mrng` above 24 + *g*; a `mova` at an `ind` not a multiple of its size | diagnostic | data | data; other bytes at a misaligned `ind` (`pocchk3.c` `m_*`) |
| Backward byte areas (steps −1, −2, −8) | data (diagnostic above the `mrng` limit) | data | other bytes from the second element on (`m_*`) |
| Misaligned base, overlapping areas | diagnostic (the 8C2, v5: a misaligned base gives the unaligned data; of two overlapping areas the first gives data, the second diagnostic) | data | misaligned: invalid value without a tag; overlap: data |
| `mova` after `eap`, after a write to `%ctpr2` | SIGILL | data | data |
| `mova` after a call | SIGILL | aborts (no signals for hardware exceptions) | SIGILL |
| `eap` then `bap` | continues | continues | restarts from the start |
| `aaurw 0, %aabf0` | movas diagnostic after the next trap | no effect | later movas invalid |
| A store to an element already prefetched | old value | stored value | stored value |
| `dpl = 1` | right half streams the left half's array | the same | right half's own fields |
| `aaurrd` | reads 0 | unimplemented, aborts | SIGILL |
| `movaq` | high half at `ind + 8` | crashes | aborts |

So APB code has to be tested on hardware, and code built by lcc with
APB (`-O2` and above) can give wrong results under MCST's qemu when the
program receives signals.

## v6 [hw: Elbrus-2C3]

`apb.c` (with the v5 cases), `apb-stream.c` and `apb-lcc.c` built by the
2C3-tuned lcc, run on the 2C3 next to the 8C2. Address arithmetic,
`am`, `ind`, `be`, narrow movas, halves, areas, `movaqp`, the stores
the buffer doesn't see, `dpl`, `dcd`, `%aabf0`, the SIGILL after a call,
a return, `eap` or a `%ctpr2` write: all as on the 8C2. What differs:

| | 8C2 (v5) | 2C3 (v6) |
|---|---|---|
| Trap (page fault, signal handler) between movas outside a loop | positions recomputed from the loop counters: the next element repeats | **positions kept**: the next `mova` continues where it was (the kernel saves `%aaldi`, above). Inside a `loop_mode` loop both are correct; an ordinary branch loop is correct only on v6 (Traps, above) |
| A `mova` outside `loop_mode` while `%lsr` has `vlc` 1, `lcnt` 0 and `ldmc` 0 (in an epilogue iteration, or after any counted loop has ended, glibc's `strncmp` included) | reads (in an epilogue iteration it is then left out of the position the kernel rebuilds: [loops.md](loops.md)) | **SIGILL `ILL_ILLOPC`** at the `mova` (`pocchk6.c` `seq`, both cores; [hwbugs.md](hwbugs.md)): write `%lsr` before such a program (0 will do) or set `ldmc` |
| `mova` wider than `fmt` | diagnostic, whatever `mrng` (`movad` on `fmt` 3 with `mrng` 8 or 16, `movaw` on `fmt` 2 with `mrng` 4, `movad` on `fmt` 1 and 2 with `mrng` 8, `movaqp` on `fmt` 1–4 with `mrng` 16, 24 or 32) | **data whenever `ind` + size ≤ `mrng`**, in all of those: the read takes its size in bytes at the area's position, which steps by the area's own element (`movaqp` from `fmt` 4 reads + 0, + 8, + 16, overlapping; from `fmt` 1 + 0, + 1, + 2), also from a base 4 bytes past a doubleword; otherwise diagnostic (`movad` with `mrng` 4, `movaw` with 2, `movaqp` with 8, or at `ind` 8 with `mrng` 16). The earlier diagnostic `movaqp` on `fmt = 4` (`tagx.c` `movaqp4`) had `mrng` 8 (`isaleft.c` `m_*`, `q_*`) |
| A byte area read by `movad` with a 12-byte step, a half area by `movaw` with a 6-byte step, `movad` at `ind` 4 of a byte area (`w12`, `w6`, `w_ind4`) | diagnostic | **the bytes at each position**, unaligned: a step need not be a multiple of the read (lcc 1.31's APB for such strides, "from Elbrus V6") |
| Diagnostic value | `eaed0f70eaed0f70`, tag 1 | `4000000040000000`, tag 1 |
| `aaurrd %aaldi0` after two `movad` | 0x40 | 0x10 (the position in bytes) |
| Bytes one area delivers a cycle | 16 | **32**: lcc's two-`movaqp` loop runs an iteration a cycle (`apb-lcc.c` sum of `long`s: 0.14 ns, 0.28 cycles, per element) |
| A line per `mova` (step 8), from L1 | a line every 2 cycles per area | a line a cycle; with 2 areas in one half 2 cycles, 4 areas (two per half) 2 cycles |
| The same from memory, one area | 3.2 cycles | 2.7 |
| Consecutive elements from memory, `asz` 0 … 5 | 10.4, 5.5, 2.9, 1.5, 1.15, 1.14 | 11.4, 5.8, 2.9, 1.47, 1.10, 1.10 |
| `mova` → consumer | (see Timing) | 5 cycles; a consumer 1–4 cycles after it stalls 4 |
| First `mova` without a stall after `bap` | 20 cycles of `nop` (`gap20`) | 18 (`gap18`) |

(`gapN` puts the first `mova` N + 2 cycles after the `bap`: 22 and 20.)

**lcc's loops enter too early on the 2C3** [hw: `tools/isa-probes/bapent.py`
and `bapent.c`, two runs, 2026-10-12]. lcc's v6 `-O3` code of
isa-score's validation kernels (`tools/isa-score/validate/kernels.c`)
issues the loop's first instruction 17 cycles after the `bap` (`sum` of
`long`s: two `movaqp` of one area an iteration; `copy` of `int`s: two
`movad` of one area) or 19 (`saxpy`: one `movaqp` from each of two
areas, one per half); the loop's `mova`s are in that instruction.
Adding empty cycles after the `bap` shows what the early start costs
(cycles a call at n = 512, less the cost had the loop started without a
stall):

| Loop's first instruction after `bap` | 17 | 18 | 19 | 20 | 21 | 22 to 25 (`saxpy` 27) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sum`, `copy`: stall | 8 | 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `saxpy`: stall | — | — | 4 | 4 | 0 | 0 |

So these loops need 19 cycles (one area) or 21 (two areas) from `bap`,
and lcc's v6 placement loses 6 cycles a call in `sum` and `copy` and 2
in `saxpy` against the best entry (the same at n = 2048, where
`saxpy`'s figure is now and then 4 cycles off). On the 4C
(`copy`, its only APB loop at `-O3`) and the 8C2 (all three, entered
at 17) the same sweep over entries 17–25 moves each loop by at most 3
cycles, mostly with a period of 4, so there entering later gains at
most 3.

lcc's loops pass on the 2C3: 0 wrong of 900 results under about 10,000
timer signals, and the guard page case; APB makes its sum 19× and its
dot product 7× faster on a 64 MiB array there.

## Not checked yet

- v6 on the Elbrus-16C. (v7 is out of scope: not in silicon.)
- Why two areas in one half make a third more DTLB misses than one in
  each half when the DTLB holds only part of their pages ("Which half
  an area is in", R = 500), and what the AAU holds that loads going to
  L2 wait for beside an area ("Plain loads beside an area"; the
  monitors name only the AAU).
